title: Polygenic risk, aspirin, and primary prevention of coronary artery disease

sections.abstract:
Recent aspirin primary prevention trials failed to identify a net benefit of aspirin for preventing cardiovascular disease vs. the harms of bleeding. This study aimed to investigate whether a high-risk subgroup, individuals with elevated genetic predisposition to coronary artery disease (CAD), might derive more benefit than harm with aspirin, compared to those with lower genetic risk.

We performed genetic risk stratification of the Aspirin in Reducing Events in the Elderly (ASPREE) randomized controlled trial using a CAD polygenic risk score (GPS Mult ). For 12 031 genotyped participants (5974 aspirin, 6057 placebo) overall, we stratified them by GPS Mult quintiles (q1–5), then examined risk of CAD (composite of myocardial infarction and coronary heart disease death) and bleeding events using Cox models. During a median 4.6 years of follow-up with randomization to 100 mg/day aspirin vs. placebo, 234 (1.9%) participants had CAD and 373 (3.1%) had bleeding events. In the overall cohort, aspirin resulted in higher bleeding risk [adjusted Hazard ratio (aHR) = 1.30 (1.06–1.61), P = 0.01] but no significant CAD reduction [aHR = 0.84 (0.64–1.09), P = 0.19]. However, among the highest quintile of polygenic risk (q5, top 20% of the GPS Mult distribution), there was a 47% reduction in risk of CAD events with aspirin [aHR = 0.53 (0.31–0.90), P = 0.02] without increased bleeding risk [aHR = 1.05 (0.60–1.82), P = 0.88]. Interaction between the GPS Mult and aspirin was significant for CAD (q5 vs. q1, P = 0.02) but not bleeding ( P = 0.80).

The balance between net benefit and harm on aspirin in the primary prevention setting shifts favourably in individuals with an elevated genetic predisposition.

Keywords: Randomized controlled trial, Aspirin, Polygenic risk score, Coronary artery disease, Genetic risk stratification
sections.introduction:
Aspirin is one of the most widely used therapies for reducing atherothrombotic cardiovascular disease (CVD) events in individuals with a prior history of CVD (secondary prevention). 1 However, use in the broader setting of primary prevention is less well-established, owing to lower event rates and increased difficulty in balancing benefits with bleeding risk. 2 Recent large aspirin primary prevention trials such as Aspirin in Reducing Events in the Elderly (ASPREE), 3 A Study of Cardiovascular Events in Diabetes (ASCEND), 4 and Aspirin to Reduce Risk of Initial Vascular Events (ARRIVE) 5 either showed no significant benefit of aspirin in reducing CVD events, 3 , 5 or a small benefit which was counterbalanced with higher bleeding risk. 4 In the ASPREE trial—a randomized, placebo-controlled trial investigating the effect of daily 100 mg aspirin on disability-free survival in 19 114 healthy older adults—there was no statistically significant reduction in CVD events in the aspirin arm, but a higher risk of major haemorrhage. 3

Despite the overall results of the ASPREE trial, it is still possible that some high-risk subgroups (e.g. stratified by lipoprotein(a) genotypes, 6 , 7 polygenic risk, or coronary artery calcium scoring 8 , 9 ) may benefit from aspirin in the setting of primary prevention—and that these benefits may outweigh the risks of bleeding in these subgroups. If biomarkers or other measures could be used to identify and stratify such subgroups, this could help guide the more personalized or targeted use of aspirin therapy in primary prevention. Polygenic risk scores (PRS) are an emerging new tool for risk stratification based on genetic predisposition, and have been used previously to stratify trial populations for statin therapy in primary and secondary prevention. 10 , 11

In the present study, we examined the performance of a multi-ancestry coronary artery disease (CAD) PRS (termed ‘GPS Mult ’) 12 for prediction and risk-stratification of CAD and bleeding events in the ASPREE trial. This new PRS incorporates genome-wide association study (GWAS) data across five ancestries for CAD and 10 CAD risk factors. We tested the performance of the GPS Mult in the ASPREE trial population, a predominately older European-ancestry population with no prior CAD events. Our objective was to investigate whether individuals with an elevated genetic predisposition (measured by a PRS) may benefit from use of aspirin in primary prevention, compared to individuals with lower polygenic risk and the overall trial population.
sections.methods:
The ASPREE trial was a randomized double-blind, placebo-controlled trial conducted in Australia and the United States (2010–17) to determine whether daily 100-mg aspirin extended the primary endpoint of disability-free survival in community-dwelling older adults. 3 , 13 The trial was undertaken in 19 114 healthy older adults aged 70 years or older (≥65 years among participants in US minority race or ethnic groups) who had no prior atherothrombotic CVD, dementia, physical disability, or other known life-limiting illness (based on their medical records at the clinics and confirmed with general practitioners) at enrolment. All participants provided written informed consent. The study was approved by the Human Research Ethics Committees at Monash University and Alfred Hospital in Australia and site-specific institutional review boards in the United States, and registered on Clinical-Trials.gov ( NCT01038583 ).

The present study involves post-hoc analysis of 12 031 genotyped participants from the ASPREE trial, a subset of participants who provided biospecimens to the ASPREE Healthy Aging Biobank for genetic analysis ( Figure 1 ). To reduce the effect of population stratification bias on the PRS distribution , 14 we exclusively included individuals with European ancestry, identified by genetic principal component (PC) analysis and overlapping the European subset of the 1000 Genomes Project phase 3 reference population. 15 Furthermore, for the non-European ancestry samples ( N = 534, 4% of all genotyped participants), there was insufficient power to test the performance of GPS Mult or undertake subgroup analyses in an ancestry-specific manner. In addition, age younger than 70 years old at enrolment and close relatives (coefficient of relatedness >0.05) were also excluded, as previously described. 16

Study flow chart indicating the selection of the final dataset. The ASPirin in Reducing Events in the Elderly (ASPREE) trial enrolled N = 19 114 individuals aged ≥70 years (≥65 years for US minorities), with no prior history of cardiovascular disease events.

The end points for this longitudinal analysis, with a mean follow-up of 4.5 years, were: (i) CAD, defined as a composite of myocardial infarction (MI) and coronary heart disease death [including death from MI, sudden cardiac death, rapid cardiac death (death shortly after possible MI), cardiac failure death with a coronary cause, and other coronary deaths], 17 and (ii) major haemorrhage (bleeding), defined as a composite of haemorrhagic stroke, symptomatic intracranial bleeding, or clinically significant extracranial bleeding (leading to transfusion, hospitalization, prolongation of hospitalization, surgery, or death). 3 All event data were collected from hospitals, medical centres, treating physicians, death certificates, and medical records, as well as from next of kin or family members where applicable. This information was forwarded to the ASPREE Data Management Center and evaluated by adjudication committees masked to randomized treatment, as described previously. 3 , 17 CAD and bleeding events were weighted equally to estimate (or attempt to quantify) the net benefit vs. harm on aspirin, per 1000 person-years. 6

DNA was purified from peripheral blood samples (buffy coat) via magnetic bead extraction and genotyped for over 850 000 genetic variant markers using the Axiom 2.0 Precision Medicine Diversity Array (Thermo Fisher Scientific, CA). Variant calling used a custom pipeline aligned to the human reference genome GRCh38 and imputation was performed based on a diverse reference panel using the TOPMed Imputation Server. 18 Post-imputation quality control (QC) removed variants with imputation quality score R 2 <0.3. In this study, we utilized the newly developed PRS GPS Mult , which integrates genome-wide association data across five ancestries (African, East Asian, European, Hispanic, and South Asian) for CAD and 10 CAD-related clinical risk factors, including body mass index (BMI), ischaemic stroke, diabetes mellitus, peripheral artery disease, glomerular filtration rate, systolic and diastolic blood pressure (DBP), low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C), and triglycerides. 12 GPS Mult has been shown to exhibit stronger associations across all ancestries and has outperformed all previously published CAD polygenic scores. 12 For the calculation, we retrieved the variant weights of GPS Mult from the PGS Catalog 19 (ID: PGS003725), which includes a total of 1 296 172 variants. After post-QC filtering in the ASPREE genotyping dataset, 1 266 464 variants were retained (excluding mismatched or redundant variants), and these were used to generate the GPS Mult distribution using PLINK software. 20

We used Cox proportional hazard (PH) regression models to estimate the association [hazard ratio (HR) and 95% confidence interval (CI)] between the GPS Mult as a continuous variable (per standard deviation, SD) and the risk of incident CAD and bleeding events. In Model 1, we adjusted for basic covariates: age at recruitment, sex, and the top 10 genetic PCs to account for population stratification. The PCs were calculated using the variance-standardized genetic relationship matrix, derived from approximately 1.2 million HapMap phase 3 variants, for the 13 349 genotyped ASPREE participants. These calculations were performed using PLINK software. 20 In Model 2, we additionally adjusted for smoking status, total cholesterol, HDL-C, systolic blood pressure, DBP, diabetes status, BMI, creatinine level, family history (in father, mother, or sibling) of MI and aspirin allocation at baseline ( Table 1 ). The GPS Mult was further investigated as a categorical variable, by dividing the GPS Mult distribution into quintile groups (q1–q5) then comprising risk of CAD and bleeding events between the lowest quintile group (q1, 0–20%) as a reference, vs. the highest quintile group (q5, 80–100%).

Baseline characteristics of ASPREE participants included in this study, stratified by the GPS Mult risk groups

SD, standard deviation; TC, total cholesterol; HDL-C, high-density lipoprotein cholesterol; LDL-C, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol; SBP, systolic blood pressure; DBP, diastolic blood pressure; BMI, body mass index; MI, myocardial infarction.

P -value was derived by a one-way ANOVA test for continuous variables or a chi-squared test for categorial variables to compare values in the three risk groups.

To assess the effect of GPS Mult on CAD risk prediction, we estimated the Harrell's C-index for a conventional model (Cox PH model) containing clinical risk (non-genetic) factors mentioned above (Model 2). Improvement in the C-index was then examined after the addition of GPS Mult to the conventional model. The likelihood ratio test was used to compare the nested Cox PH models.

We evaluated whether aspirin treatment modulated the genetic predisposition to CAD by investigating interactions between aspirin allocation and the PRS (as a continuous variable or quintile group) using the fully adjusted model (Model 2).

Subgroup analyses stratified by aspirin treatment and GPS Mult quintile groups were then performed to examine the aspirin effect on incident CAD and bleeding risk in subgroups of the ASPREE trial, respectively. Finally, we estimated the cumulative incidence of CAD and bleeding events between participants in the highest vs lowest GPS Mult quintiles, in the aspirin and placebo arms separately, adjusting for the same covariates as above. Statistical analyses were performed using R version 4.0.3.
sections.results:
The baseline characteristics of the study population are shown in Table 1 . The mean (SD) age of the participants was 75.1 (4.2) years, and 6606 (54.9%) of the participants were female. Only a small number of participants were current smokers (3.1%) and 41.5% were former smokers. After genetic stratification into PRS quintiles (q1–5) using the GPS Mult , we observed significant differences in baseline characteristics ( P < 0.001), including for age, sex, HDL-C, diabetes, BMI, and family history of MI between quintiles ( Table 1 ). For instance, 7.4% of the participants in the lowest GPS Mult quintile (q1) had diabetes at baseline, compared with 11.6% in the highest quintile (q5).

During a median 4.6 years (interquartile range: 3.5–5.6 years) of follow-up, 234 (1.9%) of the participants had incident CAD events (207 incident MI cases and 45 coronary heart disease deaths) and 373 (3.1%) had major bleeding events. In the overall cohort, 5974 participants (49.7%) were assigned to receive aspirin, and 6057 participants (50.3%) were assigned to receive placebo. Aspirin was associated with higher bleeding risk [HR = 1.30 (1.06–1.61), P = 0.01] but no significant reduction in CAD risk [HR = 0.84 (0.64–1.09), P = 0.19].

When analysed as a continuous variable, the GPS Mult was significantly associated with incident CAD risk in the overall genotyped trial population, irrespective of aspirin allocation [full adjusted HR 1.35 per SD (1.18–1.54), Table 2 ]. The GPS Mult was not associated with incident bleeding risk when analysed as a continuous variable in the overall population [full adjusted HR 0.92 per SD (0.82–1.02), P = 0.11] ( Supplementary material online, Table S1 ).

Association of the GPS Mult with incident CAD events in the overall trial population

Cox PH regression models were used to estimate the hazard ratio (HR) of the GPS Mult with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Model 1 was adjusted for age at recruitment, sex, and top 10 genetic PCs. Model 2 was additionally adjusted for baseline smoking status, total cholesterol, high-density lipoprotein cholesterol, systolic blood pressure, diastolic blood pressure, diabetes status, body mass index, creatinine level and family history of myocardial infarction, and aspirin allocation.

When analysed as a categorical variable, stratifying the cohort into quintiles of the GPS Mult distribution, we observed an over three-fold higher risk of incident CAD in the highest vs. lowest GPS Mult quintiles [full adjusted HR 3.12 (1.90–5.12), P < 0.001], irrespective of aspirin allocation ( Table 2 ). We observed no statistically significant difference in bleeding risk between the highest vs. lowest GPS Mult quintiles [full adjusted HR 0.78 per SD (0.54–1.12), P = 0.18] ( Supplementary material online, Table S1 ).

The C-index estimates for the overall trial population are shown in Supplementary material online, Table S2 , based on different models examined. The C-index of the unadjusted model for GPS Mult alone was 0.59 (0.55–0.63). The C-index of the conventional model, which contained conventional cardiovascular disease risk factors and no genetic information, was 0.72 (0.69–0.76). After addition of the GPS Mult to the model, the C-index was improved to 0.74 (0.70–0.77) ( P -value <0.001 by likelihood ratio test to compare the two models).

Supplementary material online, Table S3 presents the GPS Mult × aspirin interaction effects for incident CAD and major bleeding events in the overall trial population. When analysed as a continuous variable, there was no significant interaction detected for GPS Mult and aspirin for CAD [interaction HR = 1.22 (0.94–1.60), P = 0.13] or bleeding events [interaction HR = 1.04 (0.84–1.28), P = 0.71]. However, when the GPS Mult was analysed as a categorical variable (stratifying the cohort into quintiles and comparing q1 vs. q5) we observed a significant interaction between the GPS Mult and aspirin allocation for CAD [interaction HR = 3.51 (1.24–9.91), P = 0.02). For this same categorical comparison between q1 vs. q5 for major bleeding events, there was no interaction effect observed [interaction HR = 1.10 (0.53–2.25), P = 0.80] ( Supplementary material online, Table S3 ).

We analysed the effects of GPS Mult on incident CAD and bleeding events in the aspirin and placebo arms separately ( Figure 2 , Supplementary material online, Tables S4 and S5 ). The GPS Mult as a continuous variable was associated with incident CAD risk in the placebo group [HR = 1.45 (1.21–1.73), P < 0.001] but the effect was attenuated in the aspirin group but still significant [HR = 1.25 (1.02–1.53), P = 0.03] ( Figure 2 A ).

Association of aspirin treatment and incident CAD (a) and major haemorrhage (b) events, stratified by polygenic risk.

When analysed as a categorical variable, stratifying the cohort into quintiles (q1–5) of the GPS Mult distribution, we observed a >five-fold increase in CAD risk between quintile 1 vs. 5 in the placebo arm [q1 vs. q5, HR = 5.87 (2.60–13.30), P < 0.001]. For this same categorical comparison in the aspirin arm, the difference in CAD risk was attenuated to less than two-fold [HR = 1.89 (0.97–3.68), P = 0.06] ( Figure 2 A ). There was no significant interaction signal for major bleeding events ( Figure 2 B, Supplementary material online, Table S3 ).

In quintile 5 of the placebo arm, there were 7.3 CAD events per 1000 person-years during follow-up. In quintile 5 of the aspirin arm, this reduced to 4.8 CAD events per 1000 person-years ( Figure 3 ). Among quintile 5, there was a 47% reduction in risk of CAD on aspirin [HR = 0.53 (0.31–0.90), P = 0.02] but with no higher risk of major bleeding [HR = 1.05 (0.60–1.82), P = 0.88] ( Figure 3 ).

Effect of aspirin on CAD and bleeding events in the ASPREE trial after genetic stratification. Among 12 031 genotyped participants of European descent enrolled into the ASPirin Reducing Events in Elderly (ASPREE) trial, we used Cox proportional hazards regression to model relationships between GPS Mult and aspirin allocation with incidence of coronary artery disease (CAD) events and clinically significant bleeding (haemorrhage) events, adjusting for covariates. We tested for interaction between aspirin allocation and high vs. low GPS Mult quintile (q5).

In a cumulative incidence analysis, we observed a higher cumulative incidence of CAD events in the placebo arm in GPS Mult q5 vs. q1 ( Figure 4 A ). However, in the aspirin arm, cumulative incidence curves for CAD did not diverge between q1 and q5 ( Figure 4 B ). For major bleeding events, we observed no divergence between q1 and q5 curves in either the aspirin or placebo arm ( Supplementary material online, Figure S1 ) and no interaction effects ( Supplementary material online, Table S3 ).

Cumulative incidence of coronary artery disease (CAD) events in the ASPREE trial stratified by CAD polygenic risk.
sections.discussion:
In this study, we tested the hypothesis that aspirin may preferentially benefit individuals with an elevated genetic predisposition for the primary prevention of cardiovascular disease. We observed that in the highest GPS Mult quintile (top 20% of the GPS Mult distribution), the benefits of aspirin outweighed the harms (when weighting CAD and bleeding events equally), with 2.5 CAD events reduced per 1000 person-years on aspirin, vs. an increase of 0.4 bleeding events. This improved balance was not favourable in the overall genotyped cohort (−0.8 CAD; +2.0 bleeding events on aspirin) or the lowest GPS Mult quintile (bottom 20%) (+1.5 CAD; +1.6 bleeding events). Interaction between the GPS Mult and aspirin allocation was observed for CAD (q1 vs. q5, P = 0.02), but not for bleeding events ( P = 0.80). Our study suggests a potential benefit to a more personalized use of aspirin in the primary prevention setting, targeting treatment to high-risk subgroups rather than the overall population (where the relative benefits are lower, and do not outweigh harms).

Several recent aspirin trials have either showed no significant benefit of aspirin in reducing CVD events (e.g. ASPREE , 3 ARRIVE 5 ), or a small benefit which was counterbalanced with higher bleeding risk (e.g. ASCEND 4 ). These trials and their conclusions have been generated independently of genetic risk stratification. They have also used variable methods (trial endpoints) to quantify aspirin benefit vs. harm. Our present study, a post-hoc genetic analysis of the ASPREE trial, suggests that distinct genotypic subgroups may derive a net benefit from aspirin, using a simple benefit: harm ratio based on equal weighing of CAD vs. bleeding events. In the overall genotyped ASPREE trial population, we observed no significant reduction in CAD risk on aspirin, but a significantly higher bleeding risk. However, after genetic stratification, we observed a 47% reduction in CAD risk on aspirin in the highest GPS Mult quintile ( P = 0.02) with no change in bleeding risk ( P = 0.88). This finding suggests that genetic stratification prior to aspirin therapy can be an effective strategy to help maximize benefits and minimize harms in primary prevention. This approach would be supported by similar genetic observations from previous trials of statins 10 or PCSK9 inhibitors , 21 where the benefits of these agents were reported to be higher in individuals with elevated genetic predisposition.

We observed no evidence of a relationship between polygenic CAD risk and major bleeding events in the ASPREE trial and found no interaction between the GPS Mult and aspirin arm bleeding events in any of our analyses ( P > 0.05). This suggests that increasing polygenic CAD risk does not influence the risk of bleeding on aspirin, whereas it does affect the likelihood of benefit. Consequently, our results suggest that the overall benefit to harm ratio on aspirin shifts favourably as genetic risk increases (into a favourable outcome of net benefit), relative to the harms of bleeding which remain equivalent across genetic subgroups. This conclusion is made with the caveat of using an over-simplified and equally weighted comparison of CAD vs. bleeding events in our analysis, which does not necessarily represent the more complex clinical picture of an individual risk assessment.

Our study used an arbitrary threshold of 80% of the GPS Mult distribution (quintile 5) to define genetic high risk. We recognize this threshold could be set differentially, and that in clinical practice quintiles are not always used for cardiovascular risk stratification. Further work is required to understand the relationship between increasing genetic risk thresholds and the point at which aspirin benefit may outweigh harms in primary prevention. This balance will also be influenced by age and other cardiovascular risk factors per-individual. While we observed an increasing trend of benefit relative to harm from quintiles 1–4 of the polygenic risk distribution ( Figure 2 A ), interaction between the GPS Mult and aspirin for CAD was only significant for the q1 vs. q5 comparison. Interaction with aspirin for CAD was also not significant when analysing the GPS Mult as a continuous variable ( P = 0.13). Further studies are required to optimize appropriate thresholds for genetic risk stratification and possible targeted aspirin use.

Previously, we published a post-hoc genetic analysis of the ASPREE trial population according to Lp(a) genotypes . 6 We found a net benefit on aspirin in individuals carrying the single rs3798220-C variant (associated with elevated plasma Lp(a) levels) in ASPREE. Whilst our prior study (on the LPA gene region alone) and the present study (on genome-wide CAD-associated polygenic risk) both use genotyping to identify high-risk subgroups who may benefit more from aspirin, they are different in several important ways. First, individuals with elevated Lp(a) are a distinct subgroup compared to individuals with high polygenic CAD risk. This is illustrated by a recent analysis of the UK Biobank reporting that variation in the LPA gene region only contributes modestly to overall PRS-mediated CAD risk (7.2% of overall) . 22 This modest contribution from the LPA gene suggests that using a genome-wide CAD polygenic score captures substantially more genetic CAD risk from variation outside the LPA gene region, and that part of this variation is contributing to a differential aspirin response. Second, the previous study on LPA genotypes analysed major adverse cardiovascular events (including CAD and ischaemic strokes), whereas the present study was restricted to CAD events only (MI and coronary heart disease deaths). Neither study involved analysis of rare genetic variants (e.g. those that cause monogenic familial hypercholesterolemia) that are known to contribute to CAD risk and may further influence the aspirin response. It is possible that multiple different genetic subgroups might benefit from aspirin in primary prevention.

With regards to the use of non-genomic risk stratification strategies and aspirin in primary prevention, other approaches including coronary artery calcium (CAC) scoring could also hold promise for identifying high-risk subgroups who may benefit. Ajufo et al. 9 previously showed that individuals with a high CAC score are likely to derive a net benefit over other subgroups (albeit only in the setting of lower bleeding risk and high estimated CAD risk). In that study, higher CAC scores were also reported to be associated with a higher risk of bleeding events. It is possible that in the future, multiple different risk-stratification strategies (genetic or non-genetic) could inform the more personalized use of aspirin therapy in primary prevention.

We previously tested the performance of an older CAD PRS 23 in the ASPREE trial population . 24 In that study, we found that the older PRS was associated with CAD risk and incident events in the ASPREE population (HR = 1.24 per SD when analysed as a continuous variable) but did not interact with aspirin allocation for CAD ( P = 0.58). Our current analysis using a newer CAD PRS (GPS Mult ), which incorporates GWAS data for CAD and related clinical traits from multiple ancestries on a large scale and thus results in notably enhanced performance compared with other existing PRS , 12 suggests an improved capability of the newer GPS Mult to identify aspirin benefit, vs. the older score. PRS methods are constantly evolving, and are being refined with emerging data from increasingly larger GWAS. Moreover, the GPS Mult is also calculated based on genetic associations from ten different CAD-related clinical risk factors, rather than CAD as an outcome alone. This methodological innovation in the GPS Mult may explain some of the aspirin specificity observed using the newer score, given the differential way that GPS Mult predicts CAD risk vs. older CAD polygenic scores.

The strengths of the study included a large genotyped study population randomized to aspirin and mean 4.5 years of follow-up. The analysis included adjudicated outcomes for CAD and bleeding events by expert committees (not self-reported), 3 , 17 and use of a newly-derived PRS. 12

Limitations include that the PRS was tested only on participants of European ancestry (due to the predominance of European-ancestry participants enrolled in the ASPREE study, and to prevent population stratification biases), meaning that our findings are not necessarily generalizable to other ancestries. The stringent exclusion criteria for the ASPREE trial resulted in a healthy survivorship bias in the study population, meaning that the participants were likely to have lower overall rates of CAD than the general population within the same age group. This may have resulted in differences between in baseline characteristics between PRS quintiles, and possibly an underestimation of the true effect of the PRS in predicting late-life CAD. The analysis also included only individuals aged 70 years and older, which limits generalizability to other age groups. However, it is noteworthy that because the ASPREE cohort is comprised exclusively of older adults with no prevalent CVD at enrolment, the benefits of low-dose aspirin observed in genetically high-risk ASPREE participants may underestimate the true potential benefit in the general population, when younger and higher-risk subgroups are included. As previously acknowledged, the simple weighting of CAD and bleeding events equally (to quantify benefit vs. harm), is also a limitation.
sections.conclusion: The main implication of our study is the concept of using genetic risk stratification to improve the primary prevention of cardiovascular disease with aspirin, by identifying subgroups that are likely to benefit more than others. With this approach, the overall balance may shift favourably into net benefit for certain high-risk subgroups. Targeting aspirin to these subgroups may enable the re-purposing of a widely available and affordable preventive therapy that has failed to demonstrate a net benefit vs. harm in the overall population. Whilst the public health potential of this approach would be significant, the practical implications of implementing such an approach would be challenging, given that mass genotyping of the general population would be required. This may become possible in the future, as genomic medicine evolves and potentially becomes mainstreamed. An improved understanding of the magnitude of possible additional benefit that might be achieved in genetically high-risk subgroups will help inform future implementation and prioritization of resources.
